title: Adani Group Seeks Government Nod to Invest in Airlines, Reversing Earlier Stance
excerpt: CFO Jugeshinder Robbie Singh said India needs daily flights to rise nearly tenfold to 30,000, and the group wants to back a fund, an airline or an entrepreneur rather than run a carrier itself.
body:
• The Adani Group has asked the government to allow it to invest in the airline sector, Group CFO Jugeshinder Robbie Singh said on Friday—reversing the group's stated position as recently as July that it was not evaluating an entry into airlines.
  • Singh said more than 60 crore people in India can fly, and daily flights need to rise nearly tenfold, from about 3,200-3,300 today to 30,000.
  • The group says it would rather invest — backing a fund, an existing airline or an entrepreneur — than run an airline itself.
  • Separately, Singh said the group's airport business should be ready for a possible demerger or listing in FY28, and the group plans about $140 billion of investment over five years.

The Adani Group, which operates eight airports in India, has requested government permission to invest in the airline sector, Group Chief Financial Officer Jugeshinder Robbie Singh told reporters on Friday, in a shift from the group's public position earlier this year.

"And that's why we requested the government to at least allow us to invest, so that we can facilitate the development of airlines. Some fund, some other airline company and things like that... or an entrepreneur who wants to go into that space," Singh said on the sidelines of the India Debt Capital Market Summit in Mumbai, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

"We requested the government to at least allow us to invest, so that we can facilitate the development of airlines."

— Jugeshinder Robbie Singh, Group CFO, Adani Group

A market the group says is far too small

Singh's case rests on scale. More than 60 crore people in India can fly, he said, yet the country operates only about 3,200-3,300 flights a day against a potential of 30,000 as air travel penetration increases. The airline business, meanwhile, has narrowed to a virtual duopoly: Tata Group-led Air India and IndiGo together hold about 90 per cent of the domestic market. Disruption at IndiGo last year, which led to thousands of flight cancellations, sharpened calls for more airlines to operate in the country.

Adani's airports—including Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Lucknow, and Guwahati—handle over one-fourth of the country's air passenger traffic, which is precisely why the group's move into airlines raises a regulatory question: airport operators are generally kept at arm's length from the airlines that are their customers.

A reversal, with limits

The request marks a change of stance. In July this year, the group said it was "not evaluating any proposal to enter the airlines business," and on November 3 Adani Airport Holdings chief executive Arun Bansal ruled out entering the business, saying it is never a good strategy to compete with customers. Singh's framing keeps a version of that logic intact: the group would rather remain an investor and let an entrepreneur run the business, he said. No specific airline, fund or investment size has been announced, and the group has not said it plans to launch a carrier of its own.

The wider plan: airports listing and $140 billion capex

The airline comments came alongside a broader funding outline. Singh said the group will prepare the ground for a potential listing of its airport business, with the corporate structure expected to be ready next year, paving the way for a possible demerger or initial public offering in FY28. Non-aeronautical revenue — retail, food and beverages, advertising and other passenger services — is about 60 per cent of the airport business's revenue and is expected to rise to 65 per cent or more.

Across the group, Singh said Adani plans to invest around $140 billion over the next five years in infrastructure and energy, continue an annual equity-raising programme of about $2-4 billion, and repay around $25-30 billion of bank borrowings over the next five to ten years. What to watch next is the government's response: whether an airport operator is permitted to hold stakes in airlines, and on what conditions, will decide whether this becomes an investment or stays an aspiration.
